comparisons.title: Managed identity vs service principal
comparisons.question: An application needs to call an Azure service. Which identity should it use?

options.name: Managed identity
options.security_problem: Credentials stored in code or configuration can leak, and someone has to rotate them.
options.purpose: Give an Azure resource its own Microsoft Entra identity whose credentials Azure creates and rotates.
options.scope: Azure resources that support it. System-assigned lives and dies with one resource; user-assigned is a standalone resource you attach to many.
options.when_to_use: The workload runs on an Azure resource that supports managed identities and calls a service that accepts Microsoft Entra tokens.
options.major_difference: Nobody ever sees or stores a credential - the platform obtains tokens for the resource.
options.limitation: The platform-issued credential only works for workloads on supporting Azure resources (or Arc-enabled servers); from outside Azure, a user-assigned managed identity needs a federated credential instead. It still needs least-privilege role assignments - a managed identity with Owner is still Owner.
options.dependency: A supporting Azure resource, and role assignments on the target.
options.validation: The resource shows an identity; the app gets a token without any stored secret; sign-in logs show managed identity sign-ins.

options.name: Service principal (app registration)
options.security_problem: Something outside Azure, or a multitenant app, needs an identity that Azure cannot manage for it.
options.purpose: The local representation of an application in a tenant, authenticating with a secret, certificate or federated credential.
options.scope: Any workload - inside or outside Azure, including CI/CD pipelines and other clouds.
options.when_to_use: The workload runs outside Azure, or must act across tenants, and cannot use a managed identity.
options.major_difference: You own the credential lifecycle - unless you use workload identity federation, which removes the secret.
options.limitation: Secrets and certificates expire, leak and need rotation; owners and consented permissions must be governed.
options.dependency: An app registration (or enterprise app), a credential or federated credential, and role assignments or API permissions.
options.validation: Credentials listed with expiry dates; federated credentials preferred; sign-in logs show service principal sign-ins.

comparisons.takeaway: Prefer a managed identity whenever the workload runs on Azure. Outside Azure, use workload identity federation - on an app registration or a user-assigned managed identity - so no secret exists; a stored secret is the last resort.
comparisons.trap: Treating a managed identity as automatically least-privilege. It removes the credential problem, not the permission problem.

clues.clue: no credentials to store or rotate, app runs on an Azure VM / App Service
GitHub Actions or an on-premises job must authenticate without a secret
clues.points_to: Workload identity federation, on an app registration or a user-assigned managed identity

clues.clue: one identity shared by several resources

comparisons.title: PIM vs Conditional Access
comparisons.question: Is the requirement about how long someone holds privilege, or about the conditions of a sign-in?

options.name: Privileged Identity Management (PIM)
options.security_problem: Standing administrative access means a stolen admin account is dangerous every hour of every day.
options.purpose: Make privileged roles eligible rather than permanent, activated just in time with approval, justification and MFA, for a limited duration.
options.scope: Microsoft Entra roles, Azure resource roles and PIM for Groups.
options.when_to_use: Privilege should exist only when needed, with an audit trail and time limit.
options.major_difference: Controls *when and for how long* someone holds a role.
options.limitation: Does not evaluate device, location or risk at each sign-in; an activated role is fully usable until it expires.
options.dependency: Microsoft Entra ID P2 (or Governance) licensing; approvers and notification settings.
options.validation: Assignments show as eligible; activation history records who, when, why and for how long.

options.name: Conditional Access
options.security_problem: A correct password from the wrong device, location or risk level still gets in.
options.purpose: Evaluate signals at sign-in (user, app, device, location, risk) and require controls such as MFA or a compliant device - or block.
options.scope: Sign-ins to cloud apps by users, guests, workload identities and agents (with the right licensing).
options.when_to_use: Access must depend on the circumstances of the request.
options.major_difference: Controls *under what conditions* a sign-in gets a token.
options.limitation: Does not remove standing privilege; a compliant admin with permanent Global Administrator is still permanently privileged.
options.dependency: Microsoft Entra ID P1 or higher; policies scoped correctly and tested in report-only.
options.validation: Sign-in logs show which policies applied and their result; What If shows the expected outcome.

comparisons.takeaway: PIM reduces how long privilege exists; Conditional Access decides whether a sign-in is allowed. Strong designs use both - for example, require an authentication strength when a role is activated.
comparisons.trap: Answering "require MFA for admins" with PIM alone, or "remove permanent admins" with Conditional Access.

clues.clue: just-in-time, eligible, time-bound, approval to activate
compliant device, location, sign-in risk, block legacy authentication

comparisons.title: Azure RBAC vs Azure Policy
comparisons.question: Is the requirement about who can act, or about what any resource is allowed to look like?

options.name: Azure RBAC
options.security_problem: People and workloads can do more than their job requires.
options.purpose: Grant a security principal a role (a set of allowed actions) at a scope.
options.scope: Management group, subscription, resource group or resource; data actions for some services.
options.when_to_use: The question is who may perform an action.
options.major_difference: About the *caller*: decides whether a principal may perform an operation.
options.limitation: Does not stop an authorized person creating a non-compliant resource - an Owner can still create a public storage account.
options.dependency: Correct role choice and scope; reviews to remove overprivileged assignments.
options.validation: Check access and role assignments show the expected principals; denied actions return authorization failures.

options.name: Azure Policy
options.security_problem: Resources drift from the organisation's rules, whoever creates them.
options.purpose: Evaluate resource properties against rules and audit, deny, modify or deploy configuration.
options.scope: Management group, subscription, resource group; all resource creation and updates in scope (and existing resources on evaluation).
options.when_to_use: The question is what configuration any resource may have, regardless of who creates it.
options.major_difference: About the *resource*: applies to everyone, including Owners.
options.limitation: Does not grant or remove anyone's permissions; Audit effects only report.
options.dependency: Assignments at the right scope, the right effect, and a managed identity for Modify/DeployIfNotExists remediation.
options.validation: Compliance view shows the assignment's results; a non-compliant deployment is denied (Deny) or remediated (DINE/Modify).

comparisons.takeaway: RBAC answers "who can", Policy answers "what is allowed". Owner plus a Deny policy still cannot create the forbidden resource.
comparisons.trap: Picking a custom role to stop people creating resources in the wrong region - that is a policy (allowed locations).

clues.clue: only the network team may manage virtual networks
no storage account may allow public blob access, even for Owners
add a tag automatically / deploy diagnostic settings when missing

comparisons.title: Private endpoint vs service endpoint
comparisons.question: Must the service have a private IP address in your network, or is it enough to limit its public endpoint to your subnets?

options.name: Private endpoint
options.security_problem: A platform service reachable on the internet can be attacked or misused from anywhere.
options.purpose: Give one specific resource a private IP in your subnet, through Azure Private Link.
options.scope: One resource (and sub-resource such as blob), reachable from the virtual network, peered networks and on-premises over VPN/ExpressRoute.
options.when_to_use: The service must be reachable privately - including from on-premises - and its public endpoint can be disabled.
options.major_difference: The service gets an address *inside* your network; traffic never needs the public endpoint.
options.limitation: Does not close the public endpoint by itself; it does not authorize anyone - data-plane permissions still apply.
options.dependency: Private DNS so the name resolves to the private IP; public network access disabled.
options.validation: The name resolves to the private IP from inside the network; public network access shows Disabled; requests from outside fail.

options.name: Service endpoint
options.security_problem: You want the service's public endpoint to accept traffic only from chosen subnets.
options.purpose: Extend the subnet's identity to the service over the Azure backbone so the service firewall can allow that subnet.
options.scope: A subnet and a service type (for example Microsoft.Storage, or the cross-region Microsoft.Storage.Global).
options.when_to_use: Traffic is from Azure subnets, and restricting the public endpoint to them is enough.
options.major_difference: The service keeps its *public* endpoint; the subnet is allowed through the service firewall.
options.limitation: Not usable from on-premises by itself; applies to a whole service type, not one resource; no private IP.
options.dependency: Service endpoint on the subnet and a matching virtual network rule on the resource firewall.
options.validation: The resource firewall lists the subnet; traffic from other networks is refused.

comparisons.takeaway: A private endpoint puts the resource on your network; a service endpoint lets your subnet through the resource's public front door.
comparisons.trap: Assuming a private endpoint closes public access - you must also disable public network access, and get DNS right.

clues.clue: private IP, reachable from on-premises, disable public access
allow only these subnets through the storage firewall, no extra cost

comparisons.title: NSG vs Azure Firewall vs security admin rule
comparisons.question: Where should this traffic rule live - next to the workload, centrally for inspection, or as an organisation-wide floor?

options.name: Network security group (NSG)
options.security_problem: Inside a flat network, one compromised machine can reach everything.
options.purpose: Allow or deny traffic by IP, port, protocol, service tag or application security group.
options.scope: Subnet or network interface.
options.when_to_use: A workload needs simple, free, stateful filtering close to its resources.
options.major_difference: Distributed and address-based; no FQDN filtering or threat intelligence.
options.limitation: Cannot inspect application traffic or filter by domain name; rules are owned locally and can be changed by the team.
options.dependency: Association with the subnet or NIC; ordered priorities.
options.validation: Effective security rules on the NIC; IP flow verify names the deciding rule.

options.name: Azure Firewall
options.security_problem: Traffic crossing a boundary needs central control, domain-based rules and threat detection.
options.purpose: A managed, stateful firewall with network, application (FQDN) and DNAT rules, threat intelligence and (Premium) IDPS and TLS inspection.
options.scope: A virtual network or secured Virtual WAN hub; traffic routed to it.
options.when_to_use: Outbound internet or cross-network traffic must be filtered by FQDN, logged centrally or inspected.
options.major_difference: Central inspection point with FQDN rules and threat intelligence.
options.limitation: Only sees traffic that is routed through it; costs per hour and per GB.
options.dependency: User-defined routes (or routing intent) sending traffic to it; a Firewall Policy.
options.validation: Next hop shows the firewall; firewall logs show allowed and denied flows; a non-allowed FQDN is denied.

options.name: Virtual Network Manager security admin rule
options.security_problem: Local teams can open what the organisation forbids.
options.purpose: Centrally enforce allow, deny or always-allow rules across many virtual networks, evaluated before NSGs.
options.scope: Network groups of virtual networks (static or dynamic by policy).
options.when_to_use: A rule must apply everywhere and must not be overridable locally.
options.major_difference: Evaluated before NSGs; Deny and AlwaysAllow cannot be overridden by NSG rules.
options.limitation: Some subnets (such as Azure Firewall, Bastion and gateway subnets) are exempt; nothing applies until the configuration is deployed to the region.
options.dependency: A network manager, network groups and a deployed security admin configuration.
options.validation: The configuration shows as deployed; effective security rules include the admin rule; an NSG allow has no effect on a denied flow.

comparisons.takeaway: NSGs segment workloads, Azure Firewall inspects traffic that crosses boundaries, and security admin rules set a floor no local team can lower.
comparisons.trap: Choosing an NSG to filter outbound traffic by domain name - NSGs cannot; Azure Firewall application rules can.

clues.clue: allow web tier to reach database tier on 1433 only
allow outbound only to *.contoso.com, block known malicious IPs
block RDP from the internet in every virtual network, even if a team adds an allow

comparisons.title: Preventive vs detective controls
comparisons.question: Must the bad thing be stopped, or seen and acted on?

options.name: Preventive control (for example Azure Policy Deny, Conditional Access block)
options.security_problem: Once a risky change or sign-in happens, the damage may already be done.
options.purpose: Stop the unwanted action before it takes effect.
options.scope: The requests that pass through the control point.
options.when_to_use: The requirement says "prevent", "block" or "must not be possible".
options.major_difference: Acts before the event; nothing to investigate afterwards.
options.limitation: Only stops what it was configured for; can break legitimate work if too broad.
options.dependency: Being in the path of every request (policy scope, CA assignment, routing).
options.validation: A test of the forbidden action fails with the control's message.

options.name: Detective control (for example Defender for Cloud recommendations and alerts, Sentinel analytics)
options.security_problem: Some risks cannot be blocked without blocking business - or slip past prevention.
options.purpose: Find the condition or activity and raise it for action.
options.scope: What the control can see - assessed resources, ingested logs, protected workloads.
options.when_to_use: The requirement says "detect", "alert", "report" or "identify".
options.major_difference: Acts after (or during) the event; produces findings someone must act on.
options.limitation: Does nothing by itself; findings without owners do not get fixed.
options.dependency: Data collection, the right plans enabled, and owners or automation for findings.
options.validation: A test condition produces the recommendation or alert, and it reaches the right person.

comparisons.takeaway: Read the verb. "Prevent" points to Deny, block or a network control; "detect" points to Defender and Sentinel. Corrective controls (remediation, automation) close the loop.
comparisons.trap: Answering a "prevent" requirement with Audit, or with a Defender alert.

clues.clue: must not be able to create
notify the SOC when it happens

comparisons.title: Posture management vs workload protection
comparisons.question: Is the requirement about how exposed things are, or about attacks happening now?

options.name: Defender CSPM (posture management)
options.security_problem: Thousands of findings, and no way to know which chains an attacker could actually use.
options.purpose: Assess configuration, connect findings into attack paths, query the security graph, and assign owners.
options.scope: Azure, AWS, GCP and on-premises (Arc) resources in connected scopes.
options.when_to_use: You need prioritisation, attack paths, cloud security explorer, governance rules or agentless scanning.
options.major_difference: Shows what *could* happen.
options.limitation: Does not detect live attacks; agentless scanning needs the plan enabled by a subscription Owner.
options.dependency: Defender CSPM enabled (by an Owner), connectors for other clouds.
options.validation: Attack paths populate; cloud security explorer returns vulnerability data.

options.name: Workload protection plans (Defender for Servers, Storage, Databases, Containers, AI Services...)
options.security_problem: An attack in progress against a server, storage account or AI service goes unnoticed.
options.purpose: Detect threats against a specific service type and raise alerts.
options.scope: Resources of that type in subscriptions where the plan is on.
options.when_to_use: You need alerts about malicious activity on that workload.
options.major_difference: Shows what *is* happening.
options.limitation: Off by default and per subscription; does not prioritise posture findings.
options.dependency: The plan enabled per subscription (ideally by Azure Policy).
options.validation: The plan shows On; a simulated or test alert appears in Defender for Cloud and the Defender portal.

comparisons.takeaway: CSPM tells you what is wrong; workload plans tell you what is happening. Good hygiene without workload plans means no detection.
comparisons.trap: Expecting Defender CSPM to raise an alert for malware on a storage account - that is Defender for Storage.

clues.clue: prioritise findings, attack path, internet-exposed VM with a critical CVE
alert on suspicious access to a storage account / SQL injection attempt

comparisons.title: Secrets vs keys vs certificates in Key Vault
comparisons.question: What kind of sensitive material is it, and does the application ever need to see it?

options.name: Secret
options.security_problem: Passwords and connection strings in code or configuration leak.
options.purpose: Store any sensitive string and return it to authorised callers.
options.scope: One vault object, versioned.
options.when_to_use: The application needs the value itself - a password, API key or connection string.
options.major_difference: Key Vault hands the value back to the caller.
options.limitation: Once retrieved, the caller can copy or log it; rotation is your process.
options.dependency: An authorised identity (ideally managed) and data-plane permissions.
options.validation: The app reads the secret at runtime; no copy exists in configuration.

options.name: Key
options.security_problem: Encryption keys that leave the vault can be stolen.
options.purpose: Perform cryptographic operations (encrypt, decrypt, wrap, sign) with the key staying in the vault or HSM.
options.scope: One vault object, software- or HSM-protected; rotation policies available.
options.when_to_use: You need encryption or signing - including customer-managed keys for other Azure services.
options.major_difference: The private key material never leaves the vault; callers ask Key Vault to use it.
options.limitation: Losing or deleting the key loses the data it protects - soft delete and purge protection matter.
options.dependency: Key permissions for the calling identity; purge protection for CMK scenarios.
options.validation: The service shows the CMK in use; operations succeed without exporting the key.

options.name: Certificate
options.security_problem: Expired or unmanaged TLS certificates cause outages and weak trust.
options.purpose: Manage X.509 certificates - issuance, renewal and the private key - as one object.
options.scope: One vault object, backed by an underlying key and secret.
options.when_to_use: You need TLS or client-authentication certificates with automatic renewal.
options.major_difference: Bundles lifecycle (issuer, renewal, notifications) with the key pair.
options.limitation: Renewal depends on issuer integration; consumers must pick up the new version.
options.dependency: Certificate permissions, an issuer (or self-signed), lifetime action settings.
options.validation: Certificate shows renewal policy and next expiry; consumers present the current version.

comparisons.takeaway: Secrets are returned, keys are used in place, certificates are managed through their lifecycle.
comparisons.trap: Storing an encryption key as a secret so the app can "use it" - the point of a key is that it never leaves the vault.

clues.clue: connection string, API key, password
customer-managed key, encryption at rest, the key must never leave an HSM
TLS certificate with automatic renewal

comparisons.title: Key Vault: Azure RBAC vs access policies
comparisons.question: How should data-plane access to a vault be granted?

options.name: Azure RBAC permission model
options.security_problem: Vault access granted outside the normal role system is hard to govern and review.
options.purpose: Grant data-plane access (for example Key Vault Secrets User) as Azure role assignments.
options.scope: Vault, resource group, subscription - or an individual secret, key or certificate.
options.when_to_use: Always for new vaults - it is the default from API version 2026-02-01.
options.major_difference: Same system as all other Azure access: PIM-eligible, reviewable, scoped down to one object.
options.limitation: Role assignments take a little time to propagate; you must pick data-plane roles, not just management roles.
options.dependency: Vault set to the Azure RBAC permission model; least-privilege built-in roles.
options.validation: Access control shows data-plane role assignments; a user without one is denied the secret.

options.name: Vault access policies (legacy)
options.security_problem: Older vaults granted access in a vault-specific list.
options.purpose: Grant key, secret and certificate permissions per principal in the vault itself.
options.scope: The whole vault only.
options.when_to_use: Only for existing vaults not yet migrated.
options.major_difference: Vault-wide permissions in a separate list, outside Azure RBAC and PIM.
options.limitation: Cannot scope to a single secret; anyone who can write the vault's access policies (for example Key Vault Contributor) can grant themselves data access.
options.dependency: The vault set to the access policy model.
options.validation: Access policies list; plan migration to Azure RBAC.

comparisons.takeaway: Use Azure RBAC for Key Vault data access - it is the default for new vaults and closes the access-policy privilege escalation path.
comparisons.trap: Assuming Key Vault Contributor cannot read secrets - under access policies it can grant itself access.

clues.clue: grant an app read access to one specific secret only
clues.points_to: Azure RBAC scoped to the secret

clues.clue: make vault access PIM-eligible and reviewable

comparisons.title: Restricted Content Discovery vs Restricted Access Control
comparisons.question: Should overshared content stop appearing in Copilot and search, or should people lose access to it?

options.name: Restricted Content Discovery (RCD)
options.security_problem: Copilot and organisation-wide search surface overshared sites to everyone who technically has access.
options.purpose: Stop a SharePoint site's content surfacing in Microsoft 365 Copilot and org-wide search.
options.scope: SharePoint sites (not OneDrive).
options.when_to_use: You need to reduce exposure quickly without disrupting the people who use the site.
options.major_difference: Changes discoverability, not permissions.
options.limitation: Anyone with access can still open files directly, people still find content they own or recently worked on, and propagation can take time on large sites.
options.dependency: SharePoint Advanced Management (included with Microsoft 365 Copilot licensing).
options.validation: After propagation, a Copilot query no longer returns the site's content, but direct access still works.

options.name: Restricted Access Control (RAC)
options.security_problem: A sensitive site is reachable by far more people than should have it.
options.purpose: Limit a site to members of specified groups, overriding existing permissions and sharing links.
options.scope: SharePoint sites and OneDrive.
options.when_to_use: People outside the named groups must lose access.
options.major_difference: Changes who can open the content at all.
options.limitation: Can disrupt legitimate users who were not in the named groups.
options.dependency: SharePoint Advanced Management; the right groups.
options.validation: A user outside the group is denied, even with an old sharing link.

comparisons.takeaway: RCD hides content from Copilot and search; RAC removes access. Fixing permissions (or RAC) is the real fix; RCD buys time.
comparisons.trap: Choosing RCD when the requirement is that unauthorised users must not be able to open the files.

clues.clue: stop it appearing in Copilot without disrupting the team
only the legal group may open the site

comparisons.title: AI gateway vs Foundry guardrails vs Defender for AI Services
comparisons.question: Is the requirement about AI traffic, AI content, or detecting attacks?

options.name: AI gateway (API Management)
options.security_problem: Consumers share token capacity and model keys, and nothing between apps and models can limit or log.
options.purpose: A chokepoint in front of models (and agents, MCP tools) with token limits, content safety checks, logging and credential handling.
options.scope: Calls that are routed through the gateway; in Foundry, projects added to the gateway.
options.when_to_use: You must limit tokens per consumer, centralise keys, or moderate prompts for every app once.
options.major_difference: Acts on requests and responses as traffic.
options.limitation: Only governs traffic that goes through it; existing Foundry projects must be added.
options.dependency: API Management (or the Foundry AI gateway), policies such as llm-token-limit and llm-content-safety.
options.validation: Requests metric rises per call; a throttled consumer gets 429 while another succeeds.

options.name: Foundry guardrails
options.security_problem: Models and agents receive harmful content or injected instructions, or produce harmful output.
options.purpose: Controls (risk + intervention point + action) that annotate or block content at user input and output, and for agents at tool call and tool response (preview).
options.scope: Models and Foundry Agent Service agents the guardrail is assigned to.
options.when_to_use: You must block jailbreaks, indirect injection, harmful categories or custom terms.
options.major_difference: Acts on content; an agent's own guardrail replaces its model's.
options.limitation: Classifiers are probabilistic; tool traffic is scanned only if those intervention points have controls; some risks are model-only.
options.dependency: A custom guardrail assigned to the model or agent (defaults cannot be edited).
options.validation: A jailbreak test is blocked; the agent shows its assigned guardrail with tool response controls.

options.name: Defender for AI Services
options.security_problem: Attacks against AI services happen and nobody is alerted.
options.purpose: Runtime threat detection on prompts and responses, with alerts in Defender for Cloud and the Defender portal.
options.scope: AI services in subscriptions where the plan is on (Foundry Models such as Azure OpenAI).
options.when_to_use: You must detect jailbreak, data leakage or credential theft attempts and investigate them.
options.major_difference: Detects and alerts; it does not block the request.
options.limitation: Prompt content is masked unless suspicious prompt evidence is on; Foundry agent protection moved to Agent 365; discovery comes from Defender CSPM.
options.dependency: The plan enabled per subscription; suspicious prompt evidence on.
options.validation: A jailbreak attempt raises an alert with a redacted prompt snippet.

comparisons.takeaway: Gateway for traffic, guardrails for content, Defender for detection - three layers, three questions.
comparisons.trap: Expecting Defender for AI Services to block a prompt - it alerts. Blocking is guardrails, the gateway, or Defender real-time protection for agents (preview).

clues.clue: one app must not exhaust the token quota
scan what a tool returns before the agent uses it
SOC must be alerted to jailbreak attempts

comparisons.title: Azure Bastion vs just-in-time VM access
comparisons.question: Is the requirement to remove the public path to the VM, or to keep management ports closed until needed?

options.name: Azure Bastion
options.security_problem: Admin access over RDP/SSH needs a public IP and an open port.
options.purpose: A managed jump service that connects administrators to VMs' private IPs over TLS.
options.scope: VMs in the Bastion's virtual network and (Basic and above) peered networks.
options.when_to_use: VMs must have no public IP while admins still connect; recording sessions needs Premium.
options.major_difference: Removes the need for a public IP on the VM.
options.limitation: Does not by itself close other paths - existing public IPs and NSG allows remain until removed.
options.dependency: An AzureBastionSubnet (/26 or larger) for dedicated SKUs; the right SKU for the features needed.
options.validation: A Bastion session to the private IP succeeds; the VM has no public IP.

options.name: Just-in-time VM access
options.security_problem: Management ports left open all the time are scanned and brute-forced.
options.purpose: Keep management ports closed and open them on request, for a chosen source and duration, with an audit trail.
options.scope: VMs covered by Defender for Servers Plan 2.
options.when_to_use: Ports must be open only when an administrator needs them.
options.major_difference: Removes the *standing* open port; every opening is requested and logged.
options.limitation: Needs Defender for Servers Plan 2; a manual standing NSG allow defeats it.
options.dependency: Defender for Servers Plan 2; JIT policy on the VM.
options.validation: NSG shows deny until a request creates a time-bound allow; request history shows who asked.

comparisons.takeaway: Bastion removes the public IP; JIT closes the port when nobody is using it. They are complementary.
comparisons.trap: Picking Bastion for "ports open only when needed", or JIT for "no public IP".

clues.clue: RDP without a public IP, record sessions
open port 3389 for one hour from one IP on request

comparisons.title: Agentless scanning vs the Defender for Endpoint agent
comparisons.question: Do you need findings without installing anything, or real-time detection and response on the machine?

options.name: Agentless scanning
options.security_problem: Machines without agents (or with broken agents) have no vulnerability or secrets visibility.
options.purpose: Snapshot the disks and scan out of band for vulnerabilities, software inventory, secrets and (Plan 2) malware.
options.scope: Running machines in subscriptions with Defender for Servers Plan 2 or Defender CSPM.
options.when_to_use: Findings are needed without installing or touching the machine.
options.major_difference: No agent, no connectivity, no performance cost - but scans about every 24 hours.
options.limitation: No real-time behavioural signal - a machine with agentless only has no EDR; stopped machines are not scanned.
options.dependency: Plan 2 or Defender CSPM (enabled by an Owner); Key Vault permissions for CMK-encrypted disks.
options.validation: Software inventory or vulnerability results appear within 24 hours.

options.name: Defender for Endpoint agent (EDR)
options.security_problem: Attacks on a running machine need to be seen and stopped as they happen.
options.purpose: Endpoint detection and response, next-generation protection and agent-based vulnerability assessment.
options.scope: Machines onboarded through Defender for Servers Plan 1 or 2 (auto-provisioned by default).
options.when_to_use: You need real-time detection, investigation and response on the machine.
options.major_difference: Real-time signal from inside the OS.
options.limitation: Requires the agent installed and healthy; it is the agent, so it can be tampered with or missing.
options.dependency: Defender for Servers Plan 1 or 2 with endpoint protection on.
options.validation: The machine appears in Defender for Endpoint; test detections raise alerts.

comparisons.takeaway: Agentless and agent-based are complementary: one gives findings without touching the machine, the other gives EDR.
comparisons.trap: Treating agentless scanning as a replacement for EDR.

clues.clue: vulnerability findings without installing anything
detect and respond to attacker behaviour on the server

comparisons.title: Web Application Firewall vs API Management
comparisons.question: Is the requirement to block malicious requests, or to control which callers may use an API and how much?

options.name: Web Application Firewall
options.security_problem: Requests carrying attacks (SQL injection, cross-site scripting, bad bots) reach the application.
options.purpose: Inspect HTTP requests against managed (DRS) and custom rules and block attacks in Prevention mode.
options.scope: Application Gateway (regional) or Front Door (global; Premium for managed rules).
options.when_to_use: You must block attack patterns, bots, or rate-limit by client IP.
options.major_difference: Judges whether a request looks like an attack.
options.limitation: Starts in Detection mode (blocks nothing); a well-formed request from an unauthorised caller passes.
options.dependency: WAF policy in Prevention mode, tuned with exclusions; the right SKU/tier.
options.validation: A test SQL injection string returns 403 and WAF logs show the blocking rule.

options.name: API Management
options.security_problem: Any caller who can reach the backend can call it as often as they like.
options.purpose: A gateway that validates tokens, identifies consumers with subscription keys, applies rate limits and quotas, and holds backend credentials.
options.scope: APIs published through the gateway - only effective if the backend accepts traffic only from it.
options.when_to_use: You must require valid tokens, limit each consumer, or hide backend credentials.
options.major_difference: Judges whether this caller may make this call at this rate.
options.limitation: Advisory if the backend is reachable directly; not an attack-signature engine.
options.dependency: Policies such as validate-jwt and rate limits; the backend locked to the gateway.
options.validation: Invalid token rejected; exceeding the limit returns 429; direct backend calls fail.

comparisons.takeaway: WAF inspects for attacks; API Management decides who may call and how often. They are commonly deployed together, WAF in front.
comparisons.trap: Using a WAF to enforce per-consumer quotas or token validation - that is API Management.

clues.clue: block SQL injection and XSS
callers must present a valid Entra token, each limited independently

comparisons.title: Sentinel analytics tier vs data lake tier
comparisons.question: Will this data drive detections and hunting, or is it kept for history and compliance?

options.name: Analytics tier
options.security_problem: Detections and hunting need fast, fully featured access to recent data.
options.purpose: Store data where analytics rules, hunting, workbooks and every real-time feature work.
options.scope: Per table; 30 days by default, 90 days at no extra storage charge for Microsoft Sentinel solution tables, extendable to 2 years.
options.when_to_use: The table feeds analytics rules or frequent investigation.
options.major_difference: Full real-time capability at standard ingestion cost.
options.limitation: Expensive for high-volume, low-value telemetry.
options.dependency: Table set to the analytics tier; retention configured per table.
options.validation: Analytics rules return results against the table; retention shows in Tables.

options.name: Data lake tier
options.security_problem: Keeping years of verbose logs at analytics prices is unaffordable.
options.purpose: Low-cost long-term storage (up to 12 years), queried with KQL jobs, notebooks and search jobs.
options.scope: Per table; analytics data is mirrored to it, and total retention can extend beyond analytics retention.
options.when_to_use: High-volume, low-value logs, or compliance retention.
options.major_difference: Minimal ingestion cost; no real-time rules.
options.limitation: Analytics rules and interactive hunting do not run on it; queries are slower and charged by data scanned.
options.dependency: The data lake enabled for the workspace (part of Sentinel onboarding for customers onboarding since September 2026); table tier or total retention configured.
options.validation: A KQL or search job returns historical results; the table shows the data lake tier.

comparisons.takeaway: Detection-grade data in the analytics tier, everything else in the data lake - and total retention to keep history cheaply.
comparisons.trap: Moving a table that feeds analytics rules to the data lake - the rules stop working.

clues.clue: must be usable by analytics rules
keep seven years for compliance at low cost

comparisons.title: Sentinel automation rule vs playbook
comparisons.question: Is the requirement to route and manage incidents, or to take action in other systems?

options.name: Automation rule
options.security_problem: Analysts spend time on mechanical triage - assigning, tagging, closing known noise.
options.purpose: React to incident creation or update (or alert creation) with conditions and ordered actions.
options.scope: Incidents and Sentinel alerts in the workspace.
options.when_to_use: Assign, tag, change status or severity, suppress with an expiry, or start a playbook.
options.major_difference: Lives in Sentinel; decides whether and when.
options.limitation: Cannot reach external systems itself; alert-trigger rules can only run a playbook and, in the Defender portal, see only Sentinel alerts.
options.dependency: Microsoft Sentinel Contributor to author; deliberate rule order.
options.validation: A test incident is assigned and tagged; suppression rules show an expiration date.

options.name: Playbook
options.security_problem: Response steps need other systems - tickets, Teams, disabling accounts.
options.purpose: A Logic Apps workflow that Sentinel runs to take action anywhere Logic Apps can reach.
options.scope: Whatever its connections and identity can reach.
options.when_to_use: You need actions in Entra, ticketing, messaging or third-party APIs.
options.major_difference: Lives in Logic Apps; does the work, with its own identity.
options.limitation: Sentinel cannot run it without Automation Contributor on its resource group; its identity is a privileged object.
options.dependency: Logic Apps permissions to build; Sentinel Automation Contributor on the resource group; a least-privilege managed identity.
options.validation: Run history shows a successful run triggered by the automation rule.

comparisons.takeaway: Automation rules are the routing layer; playbooks are the action layer.
comparisons.trap: Granting Playbook Operator to someone who must build playbooks - building needs Logic Apps permissions.

clues.clue: automatically assign and tag new incidents
create a ServiceNow ticket / disable the user in Entra

comparisons.title: Windows Security Events via AMA vs Windows Forwarded Events
comparisons.question: Should each server send its own Security log, or should endpoints forward to a collector?

options.name: Windows Security Events via AMA
options.security_problem: Windows logon and process evidence never reaches the SIEM.
options.purpose: Azure Monitor Agent on each machine sends the Security log, filtered by an event set or XPath.
options.scope: Each Azure VM or Arc-enabled server with AMA and the DCR.
options.when_to_use: Machines can run AMA and reach Azure, and you want built-in Windows rules to work unchanged.
options.major_difference: Writes to SecurityEvent, which many built-in analytics rules query.
options.limitation: An agent (and Arc outside Azure) on every machine; All events is very expensive.
options.dependency: AMA, a DCR with Common, Minimal or custom XPath, Arc for non-Azure machines.
options.validation: SecurityEvent has the expected event IDs from each machine.

options.name: Windows Forwarded Events (WEF)
options.security_problem: Endpoints cannot (or should not) connect to Azure directly.
options.purpose: Endpoints forward events to a Windows Event Collector; AMA on the collector sends the ForwardedEvents channel.
options.scope: One collector (plus WEF subscriptions on many endpoints).
options.when_to_use: Many endpoints, no direct Azure connectivity, one place to run the agent.
options.major_difference: Writes to WindowsEvent - including forwarded Security log events.
options.limitation: Built-in rules that query SecurityEvent will not see this data unless adapted (or ASIM parsers are used); collecting both ways duplicates events.
options.dependency: WEF subscriptions, a collector running AMA, the Windows Forwarded Events connector.
options.validation: WindowsEvent has rows from the collector; detections that need them query WindowsEvent or ASIM.

comparisons.takeaway: Same events, different tables: SecurityEvent for direct collection, WindowsEvent for forwarded collection - and detections must read the right one.
comparisons.trap: Forwarding events with WEF and assuming the built-in SecurityEvent rules now cover them.

clues.clue: collect only these event IDs from each server
clues.points_to: Windows Security Events via AMA with custom XPath

clues.clue: endpoints must not connect to Azure directly
clues.points_to: Windows Forwarded Events via a collector

comparisons.title: On-behalf-of agent vs autonomous agent
comparisons.question: Whose token does the agent use - a signed-in user's, or its own?

options.name: On-behalf-of (delegated) agent
options.security_problem: An assistant acting for a user could reach more than that user should.
options.purpose: Act with the signed-in user's delegated permissions.
options.scope: Whatever the signed-in user can reach, limited by the delegated permissions granted.
options.when_to_use: The agent assists a person interactively.
options.major_difference: The user is the token subject, so the user's Conditional Access policies apply.
options.limitation: Reach changes with every user - a broadly privileged user widens it; prompt injection can misuse that user's access.
options.dependency: Delegated permissions and consent; least privilege for users.
options.validation: Sign-in logs show the user as subject with the agent as client; the user's policies applied.

options.name: Autonomous (app-only) agent
options.security_problem: A background agent with broad standing permissions acts with nobody watching.
options.purpose: Act as its own agent identity, with no user present.
options.scope: Exactly what the agent identity is granted.
options.when_to_use: The agent runs on its own schedule or triggers.
options.major_difference: The agent identity is the token subject, so agent-targeted Conditional Access applies - All users policies do not.
options.limitation: Needs its own governance: sponsor, expiring access, agent-specific policies; cannot do MFA.
options.dependency: Microsoft Entra Agent ID, agent Conditional Access (E7 or Agent 365 licensing), least-privilege grants.
options.validation: Agent identity sign-ins show the agent policy result; access packages show expiry and sponsor.

comparisons.takeaway: Target Conditional Access at the token subject: users for on-behalf-of agents, agent identities or blueprints for autonomous ones.
comparisons.trap: Assuming your All users MFA policy covers agents - it does not include agent identities or agents' user accounts.

clues.clue: assistant that acts for the signed-in user
nightly agent with no user present

comparisons.title: Security Copilot roles vs underlying service roles
comparisons.question: Does this role let someone use Security Copilot, or see the data Copilot reasons over?

options.name: Copilot owner / contributor
options.security_problem: The wrong people can use or administer an AI assistant connected to security tools.
options.purpose: Grant access to the Security Copilot platform (owner: administer; contributor: use).
options.scope: The Security Copilot workspace.
options.when_to_use: Deciding who may open Security Copilot, manage plugins or capacity.
options.major_difference: Platform access only - no data access by itself.
options.limitation: Does not control what data a user sees; older tenants may still assign contributor to Everyone.
options.dependency: Role assignment in Security Copilot (users and role-assignable groups); owner role selection.
options.validation: Role assignment lists the intended groups; Everyone is not assigned.

options.name: Service roles (for example Microsoft Sentinel Reader, Purview roles, Intune roles)
options.security_problem: Copilot could expose data a user should not see.
options.purpose: Grant access to each product's data, which Copilot plugins then respect.
options.scope: Each underlying service and its scopes.
options.when_to_use: Deciding what data a user (or agent identity) can retrieve through Copilot.
options.major_difference: Copilot inherits these - two users get different answers to the same prompt.
options.limitation: An empty answer may mean no access; granting a broad role (such as Security Administrator) just for Copilot over-privileges the user.
options.dependency: Least-privilege role assignments in each product.
options.validation: A user without Sentinel Reader gets no Sentinel data through Copilot; with it, they do.

comparisons.takeaway: Copilot roles open the door; service roles decide what is in the room.
comparisons.trap: Restricting Copilot contributor and believing that limits data exposure - data access was always the service roles.

clues.clue: analyst can query Purview but not Sentinel through Copilot
restrict who can open Security Copilot
